title: The Air Conditioning Investment Notebook
text:
Preface
This is a personal research notebook. Its purpose is to help me understand the air-conditioning industry — broadly defined to include cooling and the heat-pump systems that increasingly do both — well enough to judge whether some publicly traded companies are worth a closer look as investments. I am the only intended audience.

title: The Air Conditioning Investment Notebook
section: Why air conditioning
text:
Why air conditioning
Cooling is one of the few large, durable demand stories that sits at the intersection of three trends that are not going away: a warming climate, rising incomes in hot and humid countries, and electrification of heating. The International Energy Agency projects that the global stock of air conditioners will grow from roughly 1.6 billion units around 2018 to about 5.6 billion by 2050 — the equivalent of selling ten new units every second for thirty years (International Energy Agency, 2018). At the same time, regulation is forcing the installed base to become more efficient and to switch refrigerants, which compresses replacement cycles and rewards companies with the best technology.






ImportantA reality check on the growth rate



That headline 1.6B → 5.6B is a unit-stock projection over 32 years, which works out to only about a 4% compound annual growth rate — respectable but not, on its own, a thrilling number, and it necessarily decelerates as saturation rises. The more investable growth comes from two things the unit count hides: value/mix (each new unit is more expensive — higher efficiency, inverters, heat pumps, low-GWP refrigerants), and regional and sub-segment divergence (emerging-Asia first-time adoption growing double-digit, European heat-pump electrification, and AI-driven data-center cooling growing far faster than the average). Recent near-term industry forecasts cluster around a ~6% annual dollar growth rate versus that ~4% unit pace — the gap is the value-mix premium. The market chapter examines whether independent sources tell a consistent story (they broadly do) and where the fast pockets are.


The investment question is not “is demand growing” — it clearly is. The harder questions are who captures that growth, how much of each company’s business is actually exposed to it, which sub-segments and technologies grow fastest, and what am I paying for that exposure today. This notebook is organized around those questions.

title: The Air Conditioning Investment Notebook
section: How this notebook is organized
text:
How this notebook is organized
The book moves from the physical product, to the market, to the companies, and finally to a synthesis:

The technology — what air conditioning actually is, the main system types, and where energy-efficiency gains come from (inverters, ductless/VRF, heat pumps, SEER2 standards, and the refrigerant transition).
The market — how big cooling is, how fast it is growing, and how that growth splits between residential and commercial, and between the U.S., Europe, and the rest of the world.
The companies — the major public players, how AC-focused each one is, their market share and likely share of growth, and a financial-lens framework for comparing them. A separate chapter covers private firms and large conglomerates where AC is a minor segment.
Synthesis — a running watchlist and a list of open questions to drive the next round of deepening.

title: 1  What air conditioning is, and its main types
text:
1.1 Residential and light-commercial system types
Air conditioning moves heat from inside a space to outside it, using a refrigerant that is compressed and expanded in a cycle (the vapor-compression cycle). The same cycle, run in reverse, is what a heat pump uses to bring heat into a building — which is why the cooling and heating industries are converging, and why “air conditioning, broadly defined” increasingly means “heat pumps.”
For an investor, the system type matters because it determines who the customer is, how the product is sold and installed, the price point, and which manufacturers compete. The major categories are below.
Window and portable units. Self-contained boxes that cool a single room. Cheap, sold through retail, low margin, and dominated by Asian volume manufacturers (Midea, Gree, Haier) plus retail brands. Low technological moat.
Central / ducted split systems. The dominant U.S. residential format: an outdoor condenser plus an indoor coil and furnace/air handler, distributing cooled air through ducts. This is the heart of the North American market and where Carrier, Trane, Lennox, Daikin (Goodman/Amana), and Rheem compete.
Ductless mini-splits. An outdoor unit connected to one or more wall- or ceiling-mounted indoor heads, with no ductwork. Efficient, increasingly used for heating as well as cooling, and the format in which Daikin and Mitsubishi Electric are especially strong. Fast-growing in North America from a small base.
Packaged units (rooftop units, “RTUs”). Single-cabinet systems common on small commercial buildings (strip malls, big-box stores). A large, replacement-driven U.S. market.

title: 1  What air conditioning is, and its main types
section: 1.2 Commercial and applied system types
text:
1.2 Commercial and applied system types
VRF (variable refrigerant flow). Networks of indoor units served by a common outdoor system, with refrigerant flow modulated per zone. Efficient and flexible for mid-size commercial buildings; Daikin and Mitsubishi Electric pioneered it and lead it.
Chillers and applied systems. Large central plants (chillers, air handlers, cooling towers) for offices, hospitals, campuses, and data centers — the fastest-growing commercial sub-segment as AI drives data-center construction. This is the domain of Carrier, Trane, Johnson Controls, and Daikin’s Applied business, and increasingly a focus for LG and others.
District cooling and process/industrial cooling. Centralized cooling distributed to many buildings, plus refrigeration and process cooling for industry and the cold chain.






Note



Investor takeaway. The retail end (window units) is high-volume, low-margin, and commoditized. The value tends to concentrate in (1) ducted residential replacement in North America, (2) ductless/VRF where efficiency and zoning command a premium, and (3) applied/commercial and data-center cooling, where engineering content, service revenue, and recurring aftermarket are highest. Where a company sits on this spectrum largely explains its margins and multiple — a theme developed in the company chapters.








NoteData-center cooling now has its own chapter



Because it is arguably the single most investable sub-theme here, data-center cooling is covered in depth in its own chapter — including the air-vs-liquid shift and beneficiaries (Vertiv, Modine, nVent, Schneider, Carrier, Johnson Controls, LG).

title: 2  Where energy-efficiency gains come from
text:
2.1 Lever 1 — Inverter (variable-speed) compressors
This chapter is the core of the investment thesis: efficiency is not just an environmental story, it is a demand-pull story. Regulation that raises minimum efficiency and bans high-warming refrigerants forces the installed base to turn over faster and rewards manufacturers whose technology already clears the new bar. Three levers do most of the work.
A conventional compressor runs full-on or off. An inverter compressor modulates its speed to match the cooling load, avoiding the energy-hungry on/off cycling. Industry and vendor sources put the electricity savings at roughly 30–50% versus comparable non-inverter units, with the added benefits of steadier temperatures and quieter operation.1 Inverter penetration is already near-universal in Japan and high in Europe, and is rising in the U.S. as efficiency standards climb — a tailwind for manufacturers (Daikin, Mitsubishi) who built their businesses on it.

title: 2  Where energy-efficiency gains come from
section: 2.2 Lever 2 — System design: ductless, zoning, and VRF
text:
2.2 Lever 2 — System design: ductless, zoning, and VRF
Two structural inefficiencies in traditional ducted central AC are duct losses and whole-house operation. Poorly installed or leaky ducts can waste 25% or more of conditioned air, and running a whole house when only part is occupied wastes more. Ductless mini-splits eliminate duct losses, and zoning (cooling only occupied spaces) can cut energy use by up to ~40% versus central systems that condition everything at once.2 VRF extends the same idea to commercial buildings. The efficiency advantage is also a pricing advantage: these are premium-margin formats relative to commodity window units.
crumbs: 2  Where energy-efficiency gains come from

title: 2  Where energy-efficiency gains come from
section: 2.3 Lever 3 — Heat pumps replacing fossil heating
text:
2.3 Lever 3 — Heat pumps replacing fossil heating
A heat pump is an air conditioner that also runs in reverse to heat. Because it moves heat rather than burning fuel to make it, a heat pump can deliver several units of heat per unit of electricity (a coefficient of performance well above 1). Electrifying space heating roughly doubles a manufacturer’s addressable equipment per home (one machine instead of separate furnace and AC) and ties cooling demand to climate policy and electrification incentives. This is why every major “AC” company now markets itself as a heat-pump company.

title: 2  Where energy-efficiency gains come from
section: 2.4 The regulatory accelerants: SEER2 and the refrigerant transition
text:
2.4 The regulatory accelerants: SEER2 and the refrigerant transition
Two U.S. regulatory shifts are pulling demand forward right now:
Minimum-efficiency standards (SEER2). The Department of Energy raised minimum residential cooling-efficiency standards in 2023, shifting the metric to SEER2 and raising the floor — forcing higher-efficiency equipment into every new sale (U.S. Department of Energy, Energy Star, 2023).
The refrigerant phase-down. Under the AIM Act of 2020, the EPA is phasing down high-global-warming-potential (GWP) hydrofluorocarbon refrigerants (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2024). The practical effect: as of January 1, 2025, new U.S. residential systems can no longer be built with R-410A (GWP ≈ 2,088). Manufacturers have moved to low-GWP A2L refrigerants — primarily R-454B (GWP ≈ 466) for ducted systems and R-32 (GWP ≈ 675) for ductless.3 This is a once-in-a-generation forced redesign of nearly every product line.






Note



Investor takeaway. Each regulatory step does three useful things for incumbents: it (1) raises the average selling price of equipment, (2) pulls forward replacement demand, and (3) penalizes low-tech competitors who cannot meet the new standard. The risk is the mirror image — a pre-buy before a deadline can borrow demand from the following year, producing an air-pocket. (Industry data already showed sharp 2025 shipment declines in some categories after the 2023–2025 changes; that cyclicality is a key thing to size before investing.)



Open question: Worth a short page quantifying the average-selling-price uplift from SEER2 + A2L refrigerants, and the evidence on pre-buy/air-pocket dynamics? That bears directly on near-term earnings risk for Carrier, Trane, Lennox.

title: 3  Regulation, standards, and pricing power
text:
3.1 Are SEER2 standards eroding? Mostly no — but future tightening has stalled
This chapter answers two questions you raised directly: (1) are U.S. efficiency standards (SEER2) eroding under the Trump administration, and does it matter for a long-term investor; and (2) how much have the SEER2 and refrigerant changes actually raised equipment prices — the “average selling price (ASP) uplift” that can show up as a structural revenue tailwind.
The short version: the 2023 SEER2 minimum-efficiency standards are still in force and have not been rolled back. What the administration has done is freeze and challenge new and future rules, not repeal the existing floor. Three things are true as of mid-2026:
First, in February 2025 the DOE postponed the implementation dates of several Biden-era standards (touching central AC, water heaters, and other products) — a delay of future tightening, not a repeal of the 2023 baseline 1. In May 2025, Congress used the Congressional Review Act to permanently rescind standards for tankless gas water heaters, commercial refrigerators, and walk-in coolers — real repeals, but none of them residential AC/heat-pump SEER2 standards 2. Also in May 2025, DOE proposed a broad deregulatory package; it is proposed, contested, and faces near-certain litigation 3.
Second, there is a statutory backstop. The Energy Policy and Conservation Act contains an “anti-backsliding” provision that bars any new standard weaker than the one it replaces. This is why the existing SEER2 minimums are relatively safe; the practical effect of the current posture is that future tightening is frozen, not that today’s floor falls 4.
Third, ENERGY STAR survived. After signals in 2025 that it might be eliminated, industry pushback kept it funded (~$33M through FY2026) and moved it from EPA to DOE 5. Separately, federal incentives — notably heat-pump tax credits — are being wound down, which is a demand negative distinct from the standards themselves.

title: 3  Regulation, standards, and pricing power
section: 3.2 Does the regulatory stall matter for a 10–15 year investor? Largely no
text:
3.2 Does the regulatory stall matter for a 10–15 year investor? Largely no
Even if U.S. federal tightening stays frozen, three forces sustain demand for efficient equipment over your horizon:
The biggest is electricity prices. The EIA projects U.S. average residential power around 18¢/kWh in 2026, up from ~17.3¢ in 2025, and calls for the strongest multi-year electricity-demand growth since 2000 — driven heavily by data centers — with some regions (New England ~30¢, Pacific ~25¢) far above average 6. Rising bills make efficiency a consumer economic decision regardless of any mandate. Second, state standards and codes (California and others) and the broader electrification trend persist independently: U.S. heat pumps already outshipped gas furnaces in 2025 7. Third, the EU is tightening, not loosening — its revised F-Gas Regulation cuts HFC quotas hard and bans high-GWP refrigerants in new equipment on a faster schedule than the U.S., forcing the same manufacturers to keep investing in efficient, low-GWP designs 8.






Note



Investor takeaway. For a buy-and-hold horizon, treat the U.S. standards question as a second-order risk. The existing floor is protected by anti-backsliding; the durable demand drivers are rising electricity prices, state rules, EU regulation, and the economics of replacement — none of which depend on the federal administration tightening standards further. The clearer policy negative is the loss of U.S. heat-pump tax credits, which dampens near-term subsidy-driven demand.

title: 3  Regulation, standards, and pricing power
section: 3.3 The ASP uplift: how much did SEER2 + the refrigerant switch raise prices?
text:
3.3 The ASP uplift: how much did SEER2 + the refrigerant switch raise prices?
This is where regulation turns into a revenue tailwind. Two waves stacked:
The 2023 SEER2 step was widely reported to raise residential system prices by roughly 15–30%, but those figures blended the efficiency mandate with general post-2020 inflation, so attribution is imprecise. Some technical commentators argue the true engineering cost of SEER2 compliance was only a few percent, implying much of the increase was pricing power rather than cost pass-through — a claim now echoed in litigation (below).
The 2025 A2L refrigerant transition (R-410A → R-454B/R-32) has the cleanest number. Analysts at William Blair, based on distributor checks in early 2025, estimated A2L would raise HVAC equipment costs ~8–10%, and that the pricing was “sticking,” with A2L products reaching ~90% of equipment sales by spring 2025 9. Lennox publicly announced a ~10% price increase on its new R-454B residential products 10. On top of that, tariffs added an estimated further few percent.
Whether the uplift sticks as a multi-year tailwind is the key question for Carrier, Trane, and Lennox. The evidence so far says yes: HVAC equipment producer prices have risen far faster than general goods prices since 2020, and manufacturers held list prices through the 2025 volume downturn rather than discounting.






WarningA live overhang: antitrust litigation



The same pricing power that makes the ASP story attractive is now the subject of antitrust class actions. Beginning in early 2026, several price-fixing suits named Bosch, Carrier, Trane, Daikin, Lennox, Rheem, and AAON, alleging coordinated price increases and production cuts since 2020. All defendants deny the allegations, and the cases are unresolved — but this is a genuine, unquantified risk to the “ASP tailwind sticks” thesis and worth tracking 11.

title: 3  Regulation, standards, and pricing power
section: 3.4 Pre-buy / air-pocket: noise for your horizon
text:
3.4 Pre-buy / air-pocket: noise for your horizon
There was a clear 2024 pre-buy of R-410A equipment followed by a sharp 2025 destocking: combined AC + heat-pump shipments fell about 20% in 2025, and Carrier’s residential business fell ~40% in Q4 2025 as the channel worked off a multi-year inventory “overage” 12. For a 10–15 year investor this is a one-to-two-year inventory and transition distortion — it matters to 2025–2026 earnings optics and short-term traders, not to the long-run replacement-driven trajectory. I would only weight it heavily if it created a depressed entry valuation worth exploiting, or if the antitrust overhang above turned the “sticky pricing” into a liability.

title: 4  How big the market is, and how fast it is growing
text:
4.1 The headline growth story (IEA) — and its limits
The most credible top-down framing comes from the International Energy Agency. Its Future of Cooling analysis projects the global stock of air conditioners growing from roughly 1.6 billion units (c. 2018) to about 5.6 billion by 2050, with global electricity demand for space cooling tripling over the same period (International Energy Agency, 2018, 2024). By 2050 about two-thirds of the world’s households could own an AC, with China, India, and Indonesia accounting for roughly half of the global total.
As flagged in the preface, that stock projection is only about a 4% compound annual growth rate — and as a stock measure it decelerates as saturation rises. So the IEA number is the right backdrop but the wrong number to get excited about. The investable growth is faster than 4% in two places the unit count hides: value/mix (each unit sells for more) and specific regions and sub-segments (emerging-Asia adoption, European electrification, data-center cooling).

section: 4.3 The regional split: where growth actually is
text:
4.3 The regional split: where growth actually is
This is the heart of the matter. Mature markets are replacement-driven and low-single-digit; emerging Asia is first-purchase-driven and double-digit. The 2024 unit data makes the divergence concrete:






Figure 4.1: 2024 room-AC unit sales growth by region (JARN/IIR data). The R code in the collapsible box below regenerates it from data/ac_unit_growth_2024.csv.



The chart shows only regions with hard 2024 unit figures (JARN/IIR). Two big mature markets are omitted because only qualitative 2024 reads are available, but they matter for the story: the United States was low-single-digit (saturated, replacement-driven; ductless mini-splits actually fell ~3.7%), and Europe was sluggish on a cool summer — with European heat-pump sales down ~22% (a subsidy/gas-price effect, not a structural one). Treat both as “roughly flat in 2024,” not zero growth.

India: +35% (room-AC sales up ~50% during the early-2024 heatwave), ~12.5M units — the fastest-growing major market, off very low penetration.
Southeast Asia: +13.9%. The IEA projects SE Asia’s AC stock rising nine-fold from 2020 to 2040; Indonesia’s ownership (14% in 2023) could reach ~85% by 2050.
Japan: +6.2% — but >90% penetrated, so this is replacement demand in a record-hot summer.
China: room AC −2.3% domestically in 2024 (property weakness) even as exports rose ~30%; the 2025 cooling year then rebounded ~+10.8%. China is the volume-and-export giant, more cyclical than growthy on domestic penetration.
United States: low-single-digit, essentially all replacement (>90% saturated); the swing factor is the refrigerant/efficiency cycle, not new adoption.
Europe: sluggish in 2024 (cool summer) but structurally the highest-optionality region — see below.

4.4 Residential vs. commercial
By unit volume and most revenue estimates, residential is the larger end-use segment, but commercial/applied carries higher engineering content, more service and aftermarket revenue, and — for data centers — the fastest growth. For an investor, the commercial/applied tilt usually means stickier revenue and higher-quality earnings, which is part of why pure-play commercial names (Trane) command premium multiples. Data-center cooling is large enough and distinct enough that it gets its own chapter.

4.5 U.S. vs. Europe: two very different penetration stories
The U.S. and Europe are almost mirror images:

United States — saturated, replacement-driven. ~90% of households have AC, so demand is dominated by replacement and efficiency/refrigerant upgrades. Large, stable, tied to the regulatory and housing cycles.
Europe — low penetration, policy-driven runway. Only ~20% of European homes have AC (IEA, 2024–25), and the heat-pump story is even more policy-sensitive. **European heat-pump sales actually *fell ~22% in 2024, to ~2.3M units, after subsidies were cut and gas prices normalized 2 — but the policy backdrop is the bull case: the EU is running roughly 15M heat pumps short of its 60M-by-2030 target**, and ETS2 carbon pricing on heating (from 2027), the Social Climate Fund, and the phase-out of fossil-boiler subsidies all point to a structural rebound. Germany’s heat-pump association expects >30% sales growth resuming.


4.5.1 Who is positioned for European growth (your specific interest)
European heat-pump and AC growth concentrates among a recognizable set. In the German hydronic heat-pump market, Vaillant, NIBE, Viessmann (now owned by Carrier), Stiebel Eltron, and Daikin together hold ~60% share; across the broader European heat-pump market, Daikin, Carrier (Viessmann), Bosch, Panasonic, and Mitsubishi Electric are cited at roughly 44% combined 3. A localization tailwind favors incumbents with EU plants: ~73% of heat pumps sold in Europe are made in Europe. The cleanest listed ways to own European cooling/heat-pump growth are therefore Carrier (via Viessmann), Daikin (Tokyo), NIBE (Stockholm: NIBE-B), and Mitsubishi Electric (Tokyo); Bosch and Vaillant are private. This is developed further in the company chapters.






Note



Investor takeaway. Two distinct opportunity types: (1) U.S. replacement + upgrade — defensive, high-margin, regulation-pulled (Carrier/Trane/Lennox); and (2) emerging-market and European first-time adoption / electrification — higher unit growth, exposed to Daikin, Carrier/Viessmann, NIBE, Mitsubishi, and the Asian volume makers (Midea, Gree, Haier). A stock’s growth profile depends heavily on which of these it is levered to.

title: 5  Data-center cooling: the fastest-growing cooling market
text:
5.1 Why it is growing: heat density, not floor space
This is, by some distance, the highest-growth corner of “air conditioning broadly defined,” and it overlaps only partly with the residential/commercial HVAC names. It deserves its own chapter because the demand driver (AI compute), the technology (liquid cooling), and the beneficiaries (Vertiv, Modine, nVent, Schneider) are largely distinct from the broad-AC story.
The driver is rack power density. A traditional server rack drew ~10–15 kW; AI training and inference racks now run 30–50 kW commonly, and next-generation GPU racks are cited at 100–300+ kW. Air physically cannot remove heat at those densities, which forces a structural shift from air cooling to liquid cooling. So unlike the broad AC market (driven by climate and incomes), data-center cooling growth is driven by the AI capital-expenditure cycle — faster, but also more cyclical and more concentrated among a handful of hyperscale customers.

5.2 Air vs. liquid — and what is winning within liquid
The reality is hybrid: direct-to-chip liquid for the hottest GPUs, air or rear-door exchangers for the rest, immersion in select niches.
Direct-to-chip (cold plate) — the near-term winner. Coolant is piped to metal plates sitting on the CPU/GPU. It is the fastest-growing mainstream method, cited at roughly 43–47% of liquid-cooling share in 2025, and is favored in NVIDIA’s reference designs.
Rear-door heat exchangers (RDHx) — transitional. Liquid-cooled panels on the back of the rack; used as a retrofit/bridge and in hybrid halls, but limited at the highest densities.
Immersion cooling — high efficiency, slower adoption. Servers submerged in a non-conductive (dielectric) fluid. The highest projected growth rate (some estimates ~26–34% CAGR) but off a small base, held back by serviceability, fluid cost, and (for two-phase) PFAS concerns.
CDUs (coolant distribution units) — the indispensable plumbing. Every liquid deployment needs CDUs to move coolant between the facility loop and the server loops. Strong attach-rate growth across all methods, making CDU makers a relatively method-agnostic way to play liquid cooling.

section: 5.5 Vertiv (VRT) profile
text:
5.5 Vertiv (VRT) profile
What it does. Vertiv designs, makes, and services critical digital-infrastructure equipment: critical power (UPS, switchgear, busway), thermal management (precision air cooling and, increasingly, liquid cooling — cold plates, CDUs, heat rejection), integrated rack/modular systems, and lifecycle services. It carries the Liebert cooling and Geist/NetSure power brands, and traces to Emerson Network Power.
Scale and momentum (FY2025). Net sales ~$10.2B, +27.7% year over year; operating margin ~17.9%; free cash flow ~$1.9B (FCF conversion ~142%). Most striking is the order book: backlog ~$15.0B (up ~109%), with Q4 2025 organic orders up ~252% and a book-to-bill near 2.9× — roughly 12–18 months of forward revenue visibility. Management guides ~27–29% organic revenue growth for 2026.2
How cooling-focused is it? Thermal management is roughly ~30% of revenue (with power ~32%, services ~23%, IT/integrated the rest), but Vertiv does not break out a precise cooling-vs-power split, and liquid cooling is described as the fastest-growing, highest-margin part of the mix. So Vertiv is not a building-HVAC company — it is an AI-data-center infrastructure company whose cooling franchise is a major, fast-growing slice.
Competitive position and risk. Vertiv is the leading scaled “one-stop” vendor combining power + thermal + services for AI data centers — broader than pure-play coolers (CoolIT, Boyd) and more cooling-deep than power-only peers (Eaton). It has been deepening the liquid-cooling/services moat through acquisitions (PurgeRite, Strategic Thermal Labs, ThermoKey). The risks are the flip side of the thesis: the valuation is rich (see the financial chapter — ~49× EV/EBITDA, beta ~2.0), earnings are tied to the AI-capex cycle, customer concentration is high among a few hyperscalers, and competition (Schneider/Motivair, nVent, Modine) could compress liquid-cooling margins over time.






Note



Investor takeaway. Data-center cooling is the place where genuinely new technology (liquid cooling) maps onto the fastest revenue growth — and it answers your “newer technology = bigger growth” question more clearly than the residential side. But it is an AI-capex play with AI-capex risk: high growth, high multiples, high cyclicality, concentrated customers. Vertiv is the flagship; Modine and nVent are the higher-purity cooling/CDU adjacencies; the cleanest pure-plays (Boyd, CoolIT) are private.

6.3 The cleanest “AC growth” exposures
Daikin Industries — The world’s largest air-conditioning maker, operating in 170+ countries, with AC as essentially its whole business. It reported record results for the fiscal year ended March 2025 (~¥4 trillion / ~€29 billion in net sales), led by applied and commercial AC and by strength in India and Japan (Daikin Industries, Ltd., 2025). It is the purest large-cap bet on the global cooling story, but trades in Tokyo and at a premium.
Carrier Global — Spun out of United Technologies in 2020, Carrier has reshaped itself into a pure-play HVAC company: it acquired Viessmann Climate Solutions (European heat pumps) and divested its Fire & Security and commercial-refrigeration businesses (Carrier Global Corporation, 2025). That makes it one of the most direct U.S.-listed ways to own residential-plus-commercial cooling and the heat-pump transition. Reported revenue is roughly $20+ billion.
Trane Technologies — A pure-play climate company, more commercial- and applied-weighted than Carrier, plus the Thermo King transport-refrigeration franchise. ~$22.5 billion revenue (Trane Technologies plc, 2025). Frequently the market’s preferred “quality” name in the group; the question is always valuation.
Lennox International — The most concentrated North American play (~$5.2 billion revenue), spanning residential, commercial, and refrigeration, with a 2024 ductless/VRF joint venture with Samsung extending its product range (Lennox International Inc., 2025). Smaller and U.S.-centric, so more exposed to the domestic replacement and refrigerant cycle.

6.4 The “AC is a small part of a giant” names
Mitsubishi Electric — The Air Conditioning Systems & Home Products segment generated roughly $9.4 billion in FY2024 and the company is a global VRF/ductless leader (Mitsubishi Electric Corporation, 2024) — but that segment is only one part of a sprawling industrial conglomerate (factory automation, power, semiconductors). You get genuine AC leadership diluted by unrelated businesses.
LG and Samsung — Both are serious in ductless/VRF and (for LG) data-center cooling, where LG cited ~$720 million of regional orders in 2024 — but AC is a modest slice of each company’s enormous electronics revenue. Exposure is real but diluted.
Johnson Controls — Pivoting away from equipment toward commercial building solutions, controls, and service; it agreed to sell its residential and light-commercial HVAC business to Bosch for $8.1 billion (Johnson Controls International plc, 2024). After that, it is more a “smart buildings / service” story than an AC-equipment story.
Vertiv is the cleanest data-center-cooling adjacency and is profiled in full — business, segments, growth, backlog, and risks — in the data-center cooling chapter, alongside Modine and nVent. For European growth specifically, the best-positioned listed names are Carrier (via its Viessmann heat-pump acquisition), Daikin, NIBE (Stockholm), and Mitsubishi Electric, with Bosch and Vaillant relevant but private — see the market chapter.






Note



Investor takeaway. If the goal is concentrated exposure to the cooling-and-efficiency growth story via liquid public equity, the shortlist is short: Daikin (global, purest, Tokyo-listed), Carrier and Trane (U.S.-listed pure-plays), and Lennox (North-America-concentrated). Vertiv is the cleanest data-center-cooling adjacency. The conglomerates (Mitsubishi, LG, Samsung, JCI) and the Chinese volume leaders (Midea, Gree, Haier) round out the picture but each comes with a “what am I really buying” caveat.

7.2 How to read it
Trane (TT) is the quality benchmark: the best margins (18.6% EBIT) and returns (25.7% ROIC) among the diversified names, the lowest leverage (~1.0× gross debt/EBITDA), strong free-cash conversion, and a heavy recurring-service tilt (>40% of revenue is recurring/service per trade-press estimates). You rarely buy it cheap — ~26× EV/EBITDA, ~31× forward earnings.
Lennox (LII) is the cheapest and highest-quality-per-dollar of the building-HVAC names: the highest operating margin (20.1%), highest FCF yield (3.4%), lowest EV/EBITDA (18.7×) and forward P/E (22.6×). The trade-offs are slower growth (−2.7% in a down shipment year), the smallest scale, ~100% North American concentration, and full exposure to the U.S. refrigerant/replacement cycle.
Carrier (CARR) is the most “in transition”: revenue fell as divestitures (Fire & Security, commercial refrigeration) washed through, and it carries the highest leverage (3.8× gross debt/EBITDA) after the Viessmann heat-pump acquisition. Its FY2024 GAAP numbers are distorted by ~$4.5B of one-time divestiture gains — use FY2025. The thesis is a cleaner pure-play HVAC + heat-pump company once the balance sheet de-levers; the ~7% ROIC needs to rise to justify the multiple.
Daikin (6367.T) is the purest large-cap cooling bet (~92% AC) and, on these numbers, the cheapest (~10× EV/EBITDA, ~24× forward P/E) with the lowest leverage — but also the lowest margins (8.3% EBIT), a yen-translation overlay, and an event-driven valuation right now (Elliott activist stake disclosed April 2026). Cheap-looking, but margin and governance are the questions.
Vertiv (VRT) is a different animal: 28% revenue growth, the best ROIC (32%), and a huge AI-driven backlog — at the price of the richest multiple in the group (~49× EV/EBITDA, ~45× forward P/E) and the highest beta (2.0). It is a data-center-infrastructure growth stock, not a building-HVAC compounder. Detail in the data-center cooling chapter.






Note



Investor takeaway (not a recommendation). The group sorts cleanly: Trane = highest quality, full price; Lennox = best value + margins, but small and U.S.-cyclical; Daikin = purest and cheapest, lowest margins + FX/governance overlay; Carrier = transition/de-leveraging story; Vertiv = high-growth AI play at a high-growth multiple. Which fits depends on whether you want defensive compounding (TT/LII), global pure-play exposure (Daikin), a turnaround (CARR), or AI-cooling growth (VRT). For a 10–15 year horizon, the durable-quality + reasonable-price intersection is where I’d focus the next round of work.

8.1 Layer 1 — Refrigerant chemicals
Some of the most interesting investable ideas here are not the equipment makers. The forced low-GWP refrigerant transition and the rising technical content of systems create demand for two upstream layers — refrigerant chemicals and components (especially compressors and valves) — where a few firms have real pricing power and where genuine technological change and new leaders are emerging. This is the “picks and shovels” angle you asked to develop.
The AIM Act (U.S.) and F-Gas Regulation (EU) are forcing the switch from high-GWP R-410A to low-GWP A2L refrigerants (R-454B, R-32) and HFO blends. That is a multi-year demand surge for the underlying fluorochemicals — and the foundational HFO patents are concentrated in two hands.

title: 8  Picks and shovels: refrigerants and components
text:
8.1.1 Solstice Advanced Materials (NASDAQ: SOLS) — the cleanest pure-play
The single most important development for this thesis: Honeywell spun off its Advanced Materials division as Solstice Advanced Materials, which began trading on Nasdaq as SOLS on October 30, 2025 1. The refrigerant/fluorine franchise that used to be an immaterial slice of Honeywell is now a stand-alone stock. FY2025 net sales were ~$3.9B, of which refrigerants and applied solutions were ~72% (refrigerants alone ~$1.3B). Crucially, in February 2026 the European Patent Office upheld Solstice’s foundational HFO-1234yf process patent against challenges from Arkema and Chinese producers — its HFO IP portfolio runs into the mid-2030s 2. SOLS is the most direct “refrigerant transition” play.


8.1.2 Chemours (NYSE: CC) — more torque, but PFAS liability
Chemours sells Opteon HFO refrigerants in its Thermal & Specialized Solutions segment (~31% of revenue). The growth is real — FY2025 TSS sales hit a record ~$2.1B (+13%), with Opteon volumes up ~56% on the AIM Act transition 3. But Chemours carries large, partly uncapped PFAS (“forever chemicals”) liabilities: a ~$450M DOJ settlement, an ~$875M New Jersey settlement (over 25 years), a share of a ~$1.185B water-systems settlement, and unresolved personal-injury and natural-resource claims 4. So CC offers the most direct Opteon volume torque but you underwrite an open-ended legacy liability. SOLS is the cleaner play; CC is the higher-beta, litigation-encumbered one.


8.1.3 Who owns the pricing power — and the sector-wide risk
Solstice (Honeywell) and Chemours jointly dominate the foundational HFO patents and license them to others, which has historically supported pricing power. Other suppliers are more diluted: Arkema (Euronext: AKE) sells R-454B (Forane) under a Honeywell arrangement; Daikin (6367.T) is both the #1 AC maker and a major fluorochemicals/R-32 producer; Orbia/Koura (BMV: ORBIA) and Chinese producers (e.g., Zhejiang Juhua, 600160.SS) round out supply but are diluted or access-constrained.






WarningThe “is the moat permanent?” risk: TFA



HFO refrigerants degrade in the atmosphere into TFA (trifluoroacetic acid), an ultra-persistent compound now under intensifying scrutiny in Europe (2025 reports from PAN Europe and CHEM Trust). If regulators classify TFA as a problematic “forever chemical,” the HFOs themselves could eventually face restriction — a structural long-term risk to the entire HFO franchise (SOLS, CC, Arkema). This is the single biggest question mark over the refrigerant-chemicals thesis and worth tracking. It also keeps natural refrigerants (R-290 propane, CO₂) in play as a longer-term alternative.

8.2 Layer 2 — Components, especially compressors and valves
The compressor is the “engine” of every system, and valves are its nervous system. This layer is interesting because the technology is changing (oil-free magnetic-bearing compressors, propane-ready parts) and because EV thermal management is pulling the same component makers into a second, faster-growing end market.

8.2.1 The compressor map: mostly private, one big IPO to watch
The marquee names are largely private: Danfoss (Danish, incl. the Turbocor oil-free compressor), Bitzer (German), Tecumseh, Bristol. The most important development is Copeland — the former Emerson Climate Technologies, the global scroll-compressor leader, carved out by Blackstone (~$14B EV) and rebranded. Copeland confidentially filed for a U.S. IPO in November 2025 5 — it is the single most important pending listing in this space and would, for the first time, give public investors direct access to the “heart of the system.” Not yet investable; watch the IPO.
Compressor exposure available through listed parents includes Midea (000333.SZ) — owns GMCC/Welling, the world’s largest AC-compressor maker; Nidec (6594.T / NJDCY) — owns Embraco; plus LG (066570.KS) and Panasonic (6752.T).


8.2.2 Sanhua (002050.SZ / 02050.HK) — the standout listed component play
The most investable pure-ish component name is Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls. It holds >50% global share in electronic expansion valves and four-way valves — the two most critical AC valves — with FY2024 revenue ~RMB 28B (~$3.9B, +14%) and accelerating (H1 2025 net profit +39%) 6. The growth engine is EV thermal management: Sanhua has been a key Tesla thermal supplier since 2016, bridging its AC-valve franchise into autos. It completed an “A+H” dual listing in mid-2025 (Hong Kong, raising ~$1B), which improves access for international investors versus pure mainland A-shares. Its main valve competitor, Zhejiang Dunan (002011.SZ), is the #2 and also plays EV thermal.


8.2.3 Where the technology is genuinely changing (and who leads)

Oil-free magnetic-bearing compressors — Danfoss Turbocor pioneered these (now ~30 years old, >140,000 installed, up to ~40% more efficient than screw compressors, and available on low-GWP HFO-1234ze). A real efficiency edge, riding data-center chiller demand — but Danfoss is private.
EV-thermal crossover — the biggest “upstart-to-leader” dynamic: AC-component makers (Sanhua, Dunan, and Chinese specialists like Aotecar) scaling fast on EV thermal content. Sanhua is the cleanest listed way to own it.
Propane (R-290) / natural-refrigerant-ready components — a fragmented, mostly-private OEM space today; the component beneficiaries (A2/A3-rated valves and sensors) again point back to Sanhua/Dunan.

title: 10  Synthesis: watchlist and open questions
text:
10.1 The thesis in one paragraph
Cooling demand is one of the largest, most durable, climate-and-income-driven growth stories available, with the global AC stock projected to grow roughly 3.5× by 2050 (International Energy Agency, 2018). On top of that secular base sits a cyclical equipment business that is being accelerated by regulation — rising efficiency standards (SEER2) and the forced low-GWP refrigerant transition (AIM Act) — which raises selling prices, pulls forward replacement, and penalizes low-tech competitors (U.S. Department of Energy, Energy Star, 2023; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2024). The investing task is to own that growth through companies where AC is a large, high-quality share of the business, at a price that doesn’t already fully reflect it.

title: Glossary
text:
The core machine
Plain-language definitions of the technical terms used throughout this notebook. The aim is to make the company and market chapters readable without prior HVAC knowledge.
Vapor-compression cycle. The basic physics behind almost all air conditioners, refrigerators, and heat pumps. A fluid (the refrigerant) is repeatedly compressed and expanded; as it changes between liquid and gas it absorbs heat in one place and releases it in another. The whole industry is essentially variations on this one cycle.
Refrigerant. The working fluid that carries heat through the system. It boils (absorbs heat) at low pressure indoors and condenses (releases heat) at high pressure outdoors. Which refrigerant a system uses is now a regulatory and competitive battleground — see R-410A, R-454B, R-32, A2L.
Compressor. The pump at the heart of the system. It compresses the refrigerant gas, raising its pressure and temperature so it can release heat outdoors. It is the most expensive and most energy-consuming component, and the part where efficiency technology (see inverter) matters most. Think of it as the “engine” of an air conditioner.
Condenser. The outdoor heat exchanger (coil) where hot, compressed refrigerant releases its heat to the outside air and condenses back into a liquid. The “outdoor unit” you see beside a house is mostly the condenser plus the compressor and a fan.
Evaporator / indoor coil. The indoor heat exchanger where the refrigerant evaporates, absorbing heat from the room air blown across it — this is what actually cools your air.
Air handler / furnace. The indoor box that blows air across the indoor coil and pushes it through the ducts. In a heating-plus-cooling home it is often combined with the furnace (which burns gas) or, increasingly, replaced by a heat pump air handler (all-electric).
Ducts. The network of channels that distribute conditioned air through a building. Leaky or poorly designed ducts waste energy — a major reason ductless systems can be more efficient.

title: Glossary
section: System types
text:
System types
Central / ducted split system. The standard U.S. home setup: an outdoor condenser unit plus an indoor coil and air handler, connected by refrigerant lines, distributing cooled air through ducts. “Split” means the system is split between outdoor and indoor units.
Ductless mini-split. An outdoor unit connected directly to one or more wall/ceiling indoor “heads,” with no ducts. Efficient and good for zoning; a format where Daikin and Mitsubishi Electric are strong.
Packaged unit / RTU (rooftop unit). A single cabinet containing all components, often mounted on the roof of a small commercial building.
VRF (Variable Refrigerant Flow). A commercial system where one outdoor unit serves many indoor units, varying the refrigerant flow to each zone for efficiency and individual control. Pioneered and led by Daikin and Mitsubishi Electric.
Chiller / applied system. Large central cooling plants for big buildings, campuses, hospitals, and data centers. “Applied” means engineered and assembled for a specific building rather than sold as a standard box.
Heat pump. An air conditioner that can run in reverse to heat a building as well as cool it. Because it moves heat rather than burning fuel, it can deliver several units of heat per unit of electricity. Central to the electrification-of-heating story.

title: Glossary
section: Efficiency and performance
text:
Efficiency and performance
Inverter (variable-speed) compressor. A compressor that modulates its speed to match demand instead of cycling fully on and off. Saves roughly 30–50% of electricity versus older fixed-speed compressors and runs more quietly and steadily.
SEER2 (Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio 2). The current U.S. rating for cooling efficiency over a season — higher is better. “SEER2” is the updated 2023 test method that replaced the older “SEER.” Minimum SEER2 levels are set by federal regulation.
HSPF2 (Heating Seasonal Performance Factor 2). The heating-season counterpart of SEER2 for heat pumps.
COP (Coefficient of Performance). Units of heating or cooling delivered per unit of electricity consumed. A COP of 3 means three units of heat moved per unit of electricity — why heat pumps beat resistance heating and gas.
Cold-climate heat pump. A heat pump engineered (often with enhanced vapor injection) to deliver rated heating output at very low outdoor temperatures (down to roughly −13°F to −22°F), removing the main historical objection to heat pumps in cold regions.

title: Glossary
section: Refrigerants and regulation
text:
Refrigerants and regulation
GWP (Global Warming Potential). How much a gas warms the planet relative to CO₂ (which is defined as 1). Old refrigerant R-410A has a GWP of ~2,088; the new ones are far lower. Regulation is forcing the industry toward low-GWP refrigerants.
R-410A. The high-GWP refrigerant that dominated U.S. air conditioning for two decades. As of January 1, 2025, it can no longer be used in new U.S. residential systems (existing systems are still serviced).
R-454B and R-32. The low-GWP replacement refrigerants. R-454B (GWP ~466) is favored for ducted systems (Carrier, Trane); R-32 (GWP ~675) for ductless (Daikin). Both are far below R-410A.
A2L. A safety classification meaning “mildly flammable.” The new low-GWP refrigerants (R-454B, R-32) are A2L — hard to ignite, but requiring updated equipment, codes, and technician training.
HFC (hydrofluorocarbon) and HFO (hydrofluoro-olefin). HFCs are the older high-GWP refrigerant chemistry being phased down; HFOs are the newer low-GWP chemistry. Companies like Honeywell (Solstice) and Chemours (Opteon) own much of the HFO intellectual property.
AIM Act (2020). The U.S. law (American Innovation and Manufacturing Act) directing the EPA to phase down HFC refrigerants — the legal driver behind the R-410A → A2L transition.
F-Gas Regulation. The European Union’s equivalent and stricter framework, cutting HFC quotas aggressively and banning high-GWP refrigerants in new equipment on a faster timeline than the U.S.
TFA (trifluoroacetic acid). A persistent breakdown product of HFO refrigerants, now under environmental scrutiny in Europe. A potential long-term regulatory risk to the entire HFO franchise.

title: Glossary
section: Data-center cooling
text:
Data-center cooling
Liquid cooling. Cooling computer chips with liquid rather than air, necessary as AI chips produce far more heat than air can remove. Includes direct-to-chip and immersion.
Direct-to-chip (cold plate). Liquid is piped to metal plates sitting directly on the hot chips. The leading near-term liquid-cooling method.
Immersion cooling. Servers are submerged in a non-conductive (dielectric) fluid. Very efficient but operationally disruptive; slower adoption.
CDU (Coolant Distribution Unit). The pump-and-heat-exchanger skid that circulates coolant between the building’s cooling system and the server liquid loops. Required in every liquid-cooled deployment.
Rack power density. How much electrical power (and therefore heat) a server rack consumes, in kilowatts. AI has pushed this from ~10 kW toward 100+ kW, forcing the shift to liquid cooling.
